If political speech isn't protected, then what is?

So I don't know if I agree that this is really a political speech issue, as the student is still free to hold and promote their beliefs outside of the school. Before you downvoat, hear me out:

Referring to Justice Fortas, Tinker V. Des Moines Independent Community School District, the majority decision said the following:

In order for the State in the person of school officials to justify prohibition of a particular expression of opinion, it must be able to show that its action was caused by something more than a mere desire to avoid the discomfort and unpleasantness that always accompany an unpopular viewpoint.

Now, I believe that it can be shown that a child who feels bullied will not perform as well as they otherwise would, and that all students should be able to get a k-12 education, and have the school be a harrasement free environment for that. And, in the face of certain political narratives, children may be bullied more. For example, to a student who has Mexican heritage, the other children may be really nasty and bully them by saying that Trump is going to deport them and do all sorts of nasty things to their family (regardless of the truth of that statement). And, they would be able to continue harassing the child by wearing Trump MAGA gear. Conversely, children of sanders supporters may torture other kids by saying that Bernie is going to take away their home and bed, leaving them on the streets (regardless of the truth of that statement), and would pick on them by wearing sanders gear. As such, I think there is a strong argument to ban all political gear from k through 12. Now, there is an argument about teaching children about the political process, but I don't think allowing hats and shirts with political slogans 365 days a year is a necessary requirement.

So, I think it is fine that they don't want Trump gear, as long as it's a full 'No Political clothing' policy and not a no-Trump policy. My middle school and high school had similar policies except for one or two days, and there was still a wide range of beliefs, and good discussion in the relevant class rooms.

In order for the State in the person of school officials to justify prohibition of a particular expression of opinion, it must be able to show that its action was caused by something more than a mere desire to avoid the discomfort and unpleasantness that always accompany an unpopular viewpoint. Certainly where there is no finding and no showing that engaging in the forbidden conduct would "materially and substantially interfere with the requirements of appropriate discipline in the operation of the school," the prohibition cannot be sustained.

Justice Fortas, Tinker V. Des Moines Independent Community School District, majority opinion
